criteria.descriptor: Correctly identifies that low utilization with free memory means the GPU is starved/idle waiting on the CPU input pipeline or host-device syncs -- not compute-bound and not a memory problem. Every fix named (num_workers, pin_memory/non_blocking, removing per-step .item()/sync, batch size, GPU-side augmentation) is technically correct and would actually help; no incorrect claims such as blaming GPU speed or memory.

Covers all three parts of the ask: what the symptom means, how to confirm it (profiling/timing), and at least two distinct fix categories (data pipeline AND sync/batching), rather than a single lever or diagnosis alone.

Explains the producer/consumer mechanism that makes the GPU idle and justifies why each proposed change removes the stall (parallel loading, overlapped transfer, fewer syncs, more work per step). Proposes verifying the root cause before changing code.
Reads as a clear, organized diagnostic narrative using correct vocabulary (utilization vs memory, DataLoader workers, pinned memory, host-device transfer/synchronization) and stays concise.

expected_answer_points: Diagnoses that low GPU utilization with free memory means the GPU is idle/starved waiting between steps, not that the model is compute-bound or out of memory
Explains the producer/consumer mechanism: CPU-side data loading/decoding/augmentation (and host-device transfers) can't keep the GPU fed, so it stalls
Proposes confirming the hypothesis before acting -- e.g., torch.profiler/Nsight, timing the DataLoader vs the step, or feeding random tensors to see if utilization rises
Recommends DataLoader fixes: increase num_workers, and use pin_memory=True with non_blocking=True transfers (and/or prefetch_factor/persistent_workers)
Identifies per-step host-device synchronizations (.item()/.cpu()/print every iteration) as a stall source and recommends reducing/deferring them
Suggests giving the GPU more work per step (larger batch size) and/or moving augmentation off the critical path or onto the GPU
Notes a caveat/trade-off: nvidia-smi utilization is coarse, and too many workers can overload CPU/RAM, so the profiler should guide the fix
common_pitfalls: Concludes the GPU is 'too slow' and recommends a bigger or faster GPU, when the GPU is actually idle and compute is not the bottleneck
Confuses GPU utilization (the nvidia-smi %) with GPU memory usage and recommends reducing memory footprint, which does not address an idle GPU
Jumps straight to mixed precision or model/compute optimizations that shorten GPU compute -- these do not help (and can worsen the imbalance) when the pipeline is data-bound
Only increases batch size and ignores the input pipeline, or offers no way to confirm the diagnosis before changing code
Adds more per-step logging with .item()/print to 'monitor' the run, not realizing those host synchronizations are part of what stalls the GPU
Treats it as a data or model correctness bug rather than a throughput/pipeline efficiency problem
reference_answer:
Low GPU utilization (20-30%) with plenty of free memory almost always means the GPU is idle between steps rather than compute-bound. Training is a producer/consumer pipeline: the CPU loads, decodes, and augments each batch and copies it to the GPU, then the GPU runs forward/backward. If the per-batch CPU work (or host-device transfers/synchronizations) takes longer than the GPU's compute, the GPU stalls waiting for data. So the bottleneck is the input pipeline, not the accelerator.

Confirm before fixing: run torch.profiler or Nsight Systems, or simply time the DataLoader against the training step. Feeding pre-generated random tensors straight to the model is a quick check -- if utilization jumps toward 100%, the model/GPU is fine and the data path is the culprit.

Fixes, roughly in order of impact:
- DataLoader: raise num_workers so loading/augmentation runs in parallel on CPU, set pin_memory=True and copy with non_blocking=True, and use prefetch_factor/persistent_workers so batches are ready ahead of the GPU.
- Remove per-step host synchronizations: avoid calling .item()/.cpu()/print on GPU tensors every iteration -- each forces the GPU to finish and stall; accumulate metrics on-device and log periodically.
- Give the GPU more work per step by increasing batch size, and move heavy augmentation off the critical path or onto the GPU.

Caveat: nvidia-smi utilization is a coarse metric and too many workers can thrash CPU/RAM, so let the profiler decide which lever to pull.
